title: Think In Weeks, Not Days: 11 Ideas from Laura Vanderkam's Big Time
author: Jeremy Caplan
summary: Jeremy Caplan shares eleven ideas from a live conversation with productivity author Laura Vanderkam about her new book Big Time, which makes the case for time abundance. Central to Vanderkam's framework is shifting the planning unit from the day to the 168-hour week, which reveals far more discretionary time than most people realise. She advocates simple half-hour-block time tracking in a basic spreadsheet, three statistically tested work-satisfaction experiments, and deliberate 'golden hours' -- the five-hour post-dinner weekday window -- as the terrain for meaningful leisure. The 'effortful before effortless' principle argues that starting leisure with friction-requiring activities (reading, playing an instrument) before defaulting to screens produces deeper satisfaction and makes large long-term projects (all of Bach, all of Shakespeare) achievable through daily ten-page installments. Vanderkam's broader philosophy treats time management not as productivity maximisation but as life curation: reducing decisions through weekly presets, making room to say yes to unexpected opportunities, and building 'active patience' into multi-year projects.
points: The week, not the day, is the right planning unit: 168 hours minus 40 work hours minus 56 sleep hours leaves 72 hours -- 'the time-crunch feeling often results from looking narrowly at today; zoom out to the week and you will often see more room.'

Simple time tracking -- half-hour blocks, plain language categories, three check-ins daily -- creates a personal archive enabling year-over-year comparison and eliminates planning guilt by confronting actual rather than imagined time use.

Three work-satisfaction experiments with statistically significant results: spend one more hour per week on preferred tasks, spend 15 more minutes with liked colleagues, take two intentional breaks daily -- none require changing jobs or having high autonomy.

The 'effortful before effortless' rule: begin leisure with at least a few minutes of something effortful before screens; you either get absorbed, or at minimum you have spent a few valued minutes. Effortful fun is easier to sustain once started; effortless fun is hard to exit once entered.

Saying no is conventional productivity advice; Vanderkam argues the opposite -- clear space to say yes, creating mental room for yellow doors (uncertain but potentially transformative opportunities) that lead somewhere surprising.
quotes: It's never about stuffing more into our days. It's not about productivity. It's about savoring and being creatively thoughtful about what we choose to do.

When people say 'my life is a circus,' they mean chaos. Laura says that's a slander against circuses. A real circus is a super-organized performance. Nobody gets shot out of a cannon at the wrong time.
Managing mental load isn't just about getting things done. It's about staying open to what could come next, and allowing for serendipity.
Someday we will die. But on all the other days, we will not.
I thought about leaving my job. I may still do that. But now I see ways to make work better whether I quit or not.
